articleTitle: The usability assurance statement-a new ISO standard and a new approach
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on User Interfaces and Standardisation
abstract: Many groups in the world are busy defining prescriptive standards for the look, feel and behaviour of the user interface. These standards may ensure conformance to an ergonomic feature set, but they do not in themselves ensure product usability. Within ISO (International Standards Organisation) TC.159/SC4 is a working group (WG5) concerned with standards for the software user interface. A sub-group of this group is working on a standard for a usability assurance statement. Essentially this is a standard framework for agreements between producers and consumers about intended or actual product usability. The paper introduces the usability assurance statement standard. It explains the approach and why it helps assure usability. Finally, it shows how this standard compliments prescriptive approaches.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ISO standards for the user interface
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on User Interfaces and Standardisation
abstract: In the field of international standards, two groups are working on USI standards, with substantial support from national bodies such as ANSI and DIN. There are four driving forces behind the work on user system interface standards: consistency between interfaces would make it much easier for users to move from one system to another, and would reduce training time; higher quality use interfaces would result from adherence to standards designed to maximise usability; comfort of the user would be assured by providing appropriate help and error messages, and enabling the user to tailor and control the interface; and procurement and product evaluation of high quality user interfaces would be simplified by testing conformance to appropriate standards. The ISO groups TC159/SC4 and JTC1/SC18/WG9 are developing standards for minimum levels of user performance and monitoring the use interface implications of other standards.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: IBM Systems Application Architecture: Common User Access
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on User Interfaces and Standardisation
abstract: There are three sets of principles behind the IBM Common User Access (CUA), which is part of the Systems Application Architecture (SAA). There is a consistent conceptual model of the application. The user is in control at all times. The system should be usable by experts and novices. These are each described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Standardisation needs for interaction with intelligent systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on User Interfaces and Standardisation
abstract: There are strong cost, performance and safety pressures taking us towards intelligent support systems; these will change the role of the user and his information needs. The information exchange at the user interface will be at a different level (e.g. talking about goals and intentions), requiring the presentation and processing of new qualities. An important innovation will be the making of decisions at the interface, involving the need to ask 'why' questions during design. The paper defines the aspects that will need quality assurance and standardization, with the aim of encouraging research and a forum for the exchange of design experience.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The development of ISO DIS 9241 Part 2: visual display terminals (VDTs) used for office tasks-ergonomic requirements. 2. Task requirements
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on User Interfaces and Standardisation
abstract: The ISO group TC159 SC4 set up a working group to develop task requirements standards for the use of VDTs in offices. The author discusses how the activities of the group have developed. The contents of ISO/DIS 9241/2 are briefly outlined. The development of the standard has raised some interesting issues which have implications for the application of ergonomics to standards.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The HF guidelines and a user-computer interface protocol
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on User Interfaces and Standardisation
abstract: The authors introduce the published HF guidelines; then they describe a user-computer interface protocol recommended by the HF guidelines. The guidelines and protocol are compilations of useful advice which reflect the current wisdom of the human factors community. The paper illustrates selected features of the HF guidelines and the user-computer interface protocol so that they may be discussed in the context of formal standards.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A user interface model as a framework for standardization
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on User Interfaces and Standardisation
abstract: The authors explain the distinction between the user interface (UI), the sensory-motor interface (SMI) and the application interface (AI). There are two trends in human computer interface standards: SMI standardisation and software productivity. They propose a reference model based on a structuring principle, to serve as a framework for generating UI standards.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
